stances.claim: The SC's Internal Rules of May 4, 2010 -- which immediately raffle new petitions to a 'Member-in-charge' before deliberation and voting -- disregard the Constitution's unequivocal command that the Court's 'conclusions... shall be reached in consultation before the case is assigned to a Member for the writing of the opinion of the Court.'

In actual practice the 'report' that the Member-in-charge submits 'takes the form of a draft decision, to which the other justices may concur by affixing their signatures or otherwise dissent from or write separate opinions on' -- meaning the Court does not first read, study, and deliberate on the pleadings before voting, but simply relies on the draft.

The 24-month constitutional deadline for case disposition is being violated systemically: by the Court's own admission in Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019), the docket reached 14,491 cases as of Dec 31, 2016 (up from 8,741 in Jan 2007), with 3,201 having breached the 24-month constitutional deadline.

While some justices have worked diligently to dispose of their assigned cases, others have obviously not done their part; the incoming CJ should implement the Carpio plan (or a better one), and 'a little transparency' -- publicizing per-justice load and monthly outputs -- would help replace 'justice delayed is justice denied' with 'prompt at last.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban amplifies superlawyer Estelito P. Mendoza's critique -- raised in a text message responding to CJ's Sept 22 column on ICJ Judge Yuji Iwasawa and elaborated in Mendoza's 42-page March 2013 Philippine Law Journal article -- that the Supreme Court's Internal Rules (May 4, 2010) disregard the Constitution's unequivocal command that the Court's 'conclusions... shall be reached in consultation before the case is assigned to a Member for the writing of the opinion of the Court.' The Internal Rules instead raffle petitions immediately to a 'Member-in-charge' who submits a 'report' that 'in actual practice... takes the form of a draft decision' on which the others concur, dissent, or write separately -- meaning the justices do not first read, study, and deliberate before voting. Compounding the problem, CJ Panganiban argues, is the systemic violation of the 24-month constitutional deadline: in Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019), the Court admitted a 14,491-case docket (up from 8,741 in 2007) with 3,201 cases past the deadline. He urges the incoming CJ -- to succeed Bersamin after his Oct 18 retirement -- to implement Carpio's 2007 backlog-reduction plan (limit accepted cases; dispose facially-non-meritorious petitions by minute resolution) or craft a better one, and proposes 'a little transparency' -- publication of per-justice case load and monthly outputs -- so that 'justice delayed is justice denied' can give way to 'prompt at last.'
